claim: Thbs4 mRNA is induced in muscle biopsies from human patients with Becker MD, Duchenne MD, and limb-girdle MD.
source: In agreement with previous findings, Thbs4 RNA is induced in muscle biopsies from human patients with Becker MD, Duchenne MD, and limb-girdle MD (LGMD) (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) (Chen et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, and is also supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2000.

claim: Thbs4 protein is induced in skeletal muscle of Sgcd-/- mice at six weeks and three months of age.
source: Thbs4 protein is induced in skeletal muscle of each mouse model at six weeks and three months of age, along with induction of an ER stress response associated with greater cleaved ATF6α-N (nuclear form) and increased total BiP levels (Figure 1B,C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Thbs4 protein is induced in skeletal muscle of mdx mice at six weeks and three months of age.

evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Induction of Thbs4 in dystrophic skeletal muscle is associated with greater cleaved ATF6α-N (nuclear form) and increased total BiP levels.

evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data showing increased ATF6α-N and BiP in Figures 1B, 1C, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: A skeletal muscle-specific transgene was generated to overexpress Thbs4 in mice.
source: To model the known increase in Thbs4 protein that occurs in dystrophic skeletal muscle we generated Tg mice with Thbs4 protein overexpression specific to skeletal muscle (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by the schematic and Western blot data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: High levels of Thbs4 protein overexpression were observed in fast-twitch containing muscles such as the quadriceps and gastrocnemius.

evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Thbs4 protein was undetectable in uninjured skeletal muscle.

claim: Extracellular Thbs4 is rapidly internalized by cultured C2C12 myoblasts.

claim: Thbs4-expanded vesicles were highly uniform in size and more electron dense compared with similar vesicles in subsarcolemmal regions from WT muscle.

claim: The presence of the Thbs4 Tg was protective in Sgcd-/- myofibers, bringing FM1-43 dye uptake levels back to WT.
source: As expected, FDB myofibers from Sgcd-/- mice showed greater dye uptake suggesting greater injury with less efficient repair, while the presence of the Thbs4 Tg was protective in Sgcd-/-myofibers, bringing dye uptake levels back to WT (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by FM1-43 dye uptake data shown in Figure 4D and 4E.

claim: FDB myofibers from Thbs4-/- mice showed greater FM1-43 dye uptake compared with WT myofibers after laser injury.
source: FDB myofibers from Thbs4-/- mice also showed greater dye uptake compared with WT myofibers after laser injury, while double Thbs4-/- Sgcd-/- myofibers displayed an even greater injury response than either Thbs4 or Sgcd single deletions alone (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by FM1-43 dye uptake data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Double Thbs4-/- Sgcd-/- myofibers displayed an even greater injury response than either Thbs4 or Sgcd single deletions alone.
source: FDB myofibers from Thbs4-/- mice also showed greater dye uptake compared with WT myofibers after laser injury, while double Thbs4-/- Sgcd-/- myofibers displayed an even greater injury response than either Thbs4 or Sgcd single deletions alone (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by FM1-43 dye uptake data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Thbs4 overexpression provides greater stability to the sarcolemma.
source: Taken together these results indicate that Thbs4 overexpression provides greater stability to the sarcolemma, while its loss renders the sarcolemma less stable.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple functional assays including lengthening-contraction injury and laser injury experiments.

claim: Loss of Thbs4 renders the sarcolemma less stable.
source: Taken together these results indicate that Thbs4 overexpression provides greater stability to the sarcolemma, while its loss renders the sarcolemma less stable.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple functional assays including lengthening-contraction injury and laser injury experiments.

claim: Part of Thbs4-dependent protection occurs from within the myofiber.
source: More importantly, since this assay uses isolated myofibers devoid of ECM attachments, it suggests that part of Thbs4-dependent protection occurs from within the myofiber.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the laser injury assay using isolated myofibers.

claim: Thbs4 overexpression significantly accelerated ER-to-Golgi vesicular trafficking.
source: Here, Thbs4 overexpression significantly accelerated ER-to-Golgi vesicular trafficking, which was fully inhibited by co-overexpression of a dominant negative (dn) ATF6α construct (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Thbs4-mediated acceleration of ER-to-Golgi vesicular trafficking was fully inhibited by co-overexpression of a dominant negative (dn) ATF6α construct.
source: Here, Thbs4 overexpression significantly accelerated ER-to-Golgi vesicular trafficking, which was fully inhibited by co-overexpression of a dominant negative (dn) ATF6α construct (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Golgi-to-sarcolemmal trafficking rates were significantly accelerated upon Thbs4 overexpression.
source: Similarly, Golgi-to-sarcolemmal trafficking rates, measured with VSVG-enhanced green floursecent protein (eGFP) after inverse (i) FRAP, were significantly accelerated upon Thbs4 overexpression, which was again inhibited with ATF6α-dn (Figure 5B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by iFRAP data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Thbs4-mediated acceleration of Golgi-to-sarcolemmal trafficking was inhibited with ATF6α-dn.
source: Similarly, Golgi-to-sarcolemmal trafficking rates, measured with VSVG-enhanced green floursecent protein (eGFP) after inverse (i) FRAP, were significantly accelerated upon Thbs4 overexpression, which was again inhibited with ATF6α-dn (Figure 5B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by iFRAP data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Accelerated trafficking with Thbs4 was mimicked by overexpression of a constitutively nuclear (cn) ATF6α construct.
source: Furthermore, accelerated trafficking with Thbs4 was mimicked by overexpression of a constitutively nuclear (cn) ATF6α construct (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP and iFRAP data shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: Overexpression of Nell2 did not increase ER-to-Golgi trafficking rates.
source: Importantly, unlike full-length Thbs4, overexpression of Nell2 or the LamG domain of Thbs4 did not increase ER-to-Golgi or post-Golgi trafficking rates (Figure 5E,F,I,J).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP and iFRAP data shown in Figure 5E and 5F.

claim: Overexpression of the LamG domain of Thbs4 did not increase ER-to-Golgi trafficking rates.
source: Importantly, unlike full-length Thbs4, overexpression of Nell2 or the LamG domain of Thbs4 did not increase ER-to-Golgi or post-Golgi trafficking rates (Figure 5E,F,I,J).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP and iFRAP data shown in Figure 5I and 5J.

claim: Overexpression of Nell2 did not increase post-Golgi trafficking rates.
source: Importantly, unlike full-length Thbs4, overexpression of Nell2 or the LamG domain of Thbs4 did not increase ER-to-Golgi or post-Golgi trafficking rates (Figure 5E,F,I,J).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP and iFRAP data shown in Figure 5E and 5F.

claim: Overexpression of the LamG domain of Thbs4 did not increase post-Golgi trafficking rates.
source: Importantly, unlike full-length Thbs4, overexpression of Nell2 or the LamG domain of Thbs4 did not increase ER-to-Golgi or post-Golgi trafficking rates (Figure 5E,F,I,J).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP and iFRAP data shown in Figure 5I and 5J.

claim: Overexpression of just the T3R domain of Thbs4 was sufficient to accelerate ER to Golgi trafficking.
source: However, overexpression of just the T3R domain of Thbs4, which functions as the ATF6α interacting region, was sufficient to accelerate ER to Golgi and post-Golgi trafficking (Figure 5G,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Overexpression of just the T3R domain of Thbs4 was sufficient to accelerate post-Golgi trafficking.
source: However, overexpression of just the T3R domain of Thbs4, which functions as the ATF6α interacting region, was sufficient to accelerate ER to Golgi and post-Golgi trafficking (Figure 5G,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by iFRAP data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Thbs4 overexpression in skeletal muscle augmented the levels of trafficking regulatory proteins such as Sar1, Rab24, Rab6, Rab3 and Rab8.
source: Thbs4 overexpression in skeletal muscle also augmented the levels of trafficking regulatory proteins such as Sar1, Rab24, Rab6, Rab3 and Rab8, which control ER-to-Golgi and post-Golgi vesicular trafficking (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C) (Brandizzi and Barlowe, 2013; Stenmark, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and citations to Brandizzi and Barlowe, 2013; Stenmark, 2009.

claim: Thbs4 accelerates intracellular vesicular trafficking in an ATF6α-dependent manner.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that Thbs4 accelerates intracellular vesicular trafficking in an ATF6α-dependent manner, thereby suggesting at least one molecular mechanism whereby Thbs4 might enhance membrane stability through greater fluxing of vesicles to the sarcolemma.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple trafficking assays showing ATF6α dependence.

claim: Loss of δ-sarcoglycan in skeletal muscle of Sgcd-/- mice resulted in the near complete absence of the other sarcoglycans at the membrane.
source: As previously observed, loss of δ-sarcoglycan in skeletal muscle of Sgcd-/- mice resulted in the near complete absence of the other sarcoglycans at the membrane (as they all form a complex; Figure 6A) (Durbeej and Campbell, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6A and a citation to Durbeej and Campbell, 2002.

claim: Thbs4 Tg alone displayed increased sarcolemmal levels of β-dystroglycan, dystrophin and β1D-integrin.
source: Interestingly, Thbs4 Tg alone displayed increased sarcolemmal levels of β-dystroglycan, dystrophin and β1D-integrin (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The Thbs4 Tg in the Sgcd deficient background resulted in greater membrane localization of α-, β-, and γ-sarcoglycan and β-dystroglycan.
source: More importantly, the Thbs4 Tg in the Sgcd deficient background resulted in greater membrane localization of α-, β-, and γ-sarcoglycan and β-dystroglycan, as well as in dystrophin, utrophin and β1D-integrin (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The Thbs4 Tg in the Sgcd deficient background resulted in greater membrane localization of dystrophin, utrophin and β1D-integrin.
source: More importantly, the Thbs4 Tg in the Sgcd deficient background resulted in greater membrane localization of α-, β-, and γ-sarcoglycan and β-dystroglycan, as well as in dystrophin, utrophin and β1D-integrin (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The Thbs4 Tg alone gave increased membrane levels of utrophin, α- and β-dystroglycan, as well as β1D-, α7 and α5-integrins compared to WT controls.
source: More quantitative assessment of this effect by Western blotting of membrane-specific protein extracts showed that even the Thbs4 Tg alone gave increased membrane levels of utrophin, α- and β-dystroglycan, as well as β1D-, α7 and α5-integrins compared to WT controls (Figure 6B; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B; red boxes), which likely explains our earlier observations whereby Thbs4 Tg skeletal muscle was protected from lengthening-contraction injury and laser injury in isolated myofibers versus WT.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The Thbs4 Tg augmented the membrane residency of attachment proteins in the Sgcd-/- background.
source: The Thbs4 Tg also augmented the membrane residency of these same proteins in the Sgcd-/- and mdx background, as well as increased membrane levels of α-sarcoglycan and β-sarcoglycan in skeletal muscle of Sgcd-/- mice (Figure 6B; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B, for replicate samples).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The Thbs4 Tg augmented the membrane residency of attachment proteins in the mdx background.
source: The Thbs4 Tg also augmented the membrane residency of these same proteins in the Sgcd-/- and mdx background, as well as increased membrane levels of α-sarcoglycan and β-sarcoglycan in skeletal muscle of Sgcd-/- mice (Figure 6B; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B, for replicate samples).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The Thbs4 Tg increased membrane levels of α-sarcoglycan and β-sarcoglycan in skeletal muscle of Sgcd-/- mice.
source: The Thbs4 Tg also augmented the membrane residency of these same proteins in the Sgcd-/- and mdx background, as well as increased membrane levels of α-sarcoglycan and β-sarcoglycan in skeletal muscle of Sgcd-/- mice (Figure 6B; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B, for replicate samples).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Expression of β1- and α7-integrin from total cytoplasmic protein extracts was not increased by Thbs4 overexpression.
source: Furthermore, we observed that expression of β1- and α7-integrin from total cytoplasmic protein extracts was not increased, suggesting that Thbs4 overexpression directly augmented membrane trafficking and localization of these critical attachment proteins to the surface (Figure 6B, lower panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6B, lower panel.

claim: Thbs4 overexpression directly augmented membrane trafficking and localization of critical attachment proteins to the surface.
source: Furthermore, we observed that expression of β1- and α7-integrin from total cytoplasmic protein extracts was not increased, suggesting that Thbs4 overexpression directly augmented membrane trafficking and localization of these critical attachment proteins to the surface (Figure 6B, lower panel).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that total protein levels did not increase while membrane levels did.

claim: Loss of Thbs4 in skeletal muscle partially reduced membrane residency of α- and β-dystroglycan, β1D- and α7-integrins.
source: Finally, we also observed that loss of Thbs4 in skeletal muscle partially reduced membrane residency of α- and β-dystroglycan, β1D- and α7-integrins (Figure 6C, burgundy boxes).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Thbs4 regulates membrane stability in skeletal muscle by augmenting the trafficking of membrane attachment protein complexes to the sarcolemma.
source: Collectively, these observations solidify a mechanism whereby Thbs4 regulates membrane stability in skeletal muscle by augmenting the trafficking of membrane attachment protein complexes to the sarcolemma.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple observations including membrane protein localization and trafficking assays.

claim: Thbs4 could directly bind intracellular β1D-integrin in primary neonatal rat cardiomyocytes.
source: As previously reported with other Thbs proteins (Adams and Lawler, 2011), we observed that Thbs4 could directly bind intracellular β1D-integrin, but not α7-integrin, in primary neonatal rat cardiomyocytes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C and a citation to Adams and Lawler, 2011.

claim: Thbs4 could not directly bind intracellular α7-integrin in primary neonatal rat cardiomyocytes.
source: As previously reported with other Thbs proteins (Adams and Lawler, 2011), we observed that Thbs4 could directly bind intracellular β1D-integrin, but not α7-integrin, in primary neonatal rat cardiomyocytes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Both Thbs4 and α5-integrin localized to β1D-integrin-positive intracellular vesicles in WT, Thbs4 Tg and Sgcd-/- quadriceps muscle.
source: In addition, both Thbs4 and α5-integrin localized to β1D-integrin-positive intracellular vesicles in WT, Thbs4 Tg and Sgcd-/- quadriceps muscle, placing Thbs4 within the same vesicles and intracellular compartment as the attachment proteins themselves (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: ATF6α was previously shown to expand the ER and post-ER vesicular compartment when activated or overexpressed.
source: Indeed, ATF6α was previously shown to expand the ER and post-ER vesicular compartment when activated or overexpressed (Brody et al., 2016; Lynch et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brody et al., 2016; Lynch et al., 2012.

claim: Skeletal muscle-specific Tg mice overexpressing ATF6α showed high levels of nuclear ATF6α protein and induction of BiP, PDI and calreticulin.
source: Thus, to directly test this hypothesis we generated skeletal muscle-specific Tg mice overexpressing ATF6α, which showed high levels of nuclear ATF6α protein and induction of BiP, PDI and calreticulin as compared to WT levels, all without influencing Thbs4 protein expression levels (Figure 7A,B; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7A, 7B, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: ATF6α overexpression in skeletal muscle did not influence Thbs4 protein expression levels.
source: Thus, to directly test this hypothesis we generated skeletal muscle-specific Tg mice overexpressing ATF6α, which showed high levels of nuclear ATF6α protein and induction of BiP, PDI and calreticulin as compared to WT levels, all without influencing Thbs4 protein expression levels (Figure 7A,B; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: ATF6α skeletal muscle-specific Tg mice appeared overtly normal and showed no histopathology of skeletal muscles.
source: ATF6α skeletal muscle-specific Tg mice appeared overtly normal and showed no histopathology of skeletal muscles (Figure 7C; Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: Ultrastructural analysis of skeletal muscle from ATF6α Tg mice showed a remarkable expansion of ER and the sub-sarcolemmal vesicular compartment.
source: Similar to Thbs4 Tg mice, ultrastructural analysis of skeletal muscle from ATF6α Tg mice showed a remarkable expansion of ER and the sub-sarcolemmal vesicular compartment, although these ATF6α-dependent vesicles appeared less dense in comparison to those observed in Thbs4 Tg mice (Figure 7D versus Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: ATF6α-dependent vesicles appeared less dense in comparison to those observed in Thbs4 Tg mice.
source: Similar to Thbs4 Tg mice, ultrastructural analysis of skeletal muscle from ATF6α Tg mice showed a remarkable expansion of ER and the sub-sarcolemmal vesicular compartment, although these ATF6α-dependent vesicles appeared less dense in comparison to those observed in Thbs4 Tg mice (Figure 7D versus Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7D and Figure 1G.

claim: ATF6α overexpression in the Sgcd-/- or mdx dystrophic background provided no protection whatsoever.
source: However, ATF6α overexpression in the Sgcd-/- or mdx dystrophic background provided no protection whatsoever (Figure 7E–J; Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological, biochemical, and functional data shown in Figure 7E–J and Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–D.

claim: ATF6α overexpression did not increase the sarcolemmal localization of any of the membrane attachment proteins observed with Thbs4 overexpression in skeletal muscle.
source: More importantly, ATF6α overexpression did not increase the sarcolemmal localization of any of the membrane attachment proteins observed with Thbs4 overexpression in skeletal muscle (Figure 7K).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7K.

claim: ATF6α is only one part of a more integrated mechanism whereby Thbs4 regulates membrane stability of skeletal muscle.
source: Hence, our data indicate that ATF6α is only one part of a more integrated mechanism whereby Thbs4 regulates membrane stability of skeletal muscle.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that ATF6α overexpression alone is not protective despite expanding vesicles.

claim: Only the secretion competent full-length Thbs4, but not the full-length ER-retained Thbs4 mutant, promoted greater β1 integrin membrane occupancy.
source: The data showed that only the secretion competent full-length Thbs4, but not the full-length ER-retained Thbs4 mutant, promoted greater β1 integrin membrane occupancy (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: Thbs4 must move through the secretory pathway to chaperone at least β1 integrin to the sarcolemma.
source: Hence, Thbs4 must move through the secretory pathway to chaperone at least β1 integrin to the sarcolemma.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that the ER-retained Thbs4 mutant does not promote β1 integrin membrane occupancy.

claim: Drosophila have a single Tsp gene that when deficient causes embryonic lethality due to ruptures in tendon/muscle attachments.
source: Our results in mice were reminiscent of data from Drosophila, which have a single Tsp gene that when deficient causes embryonic lethality due to ruptures in tendon/muscle attachments (Subramanian et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Subramanian et al., 2007.

claim: Tsp in Drosophila was shown to interact with αPS2/βPS integrin.
source: Moreover, Tsp in Drosophila was also shown to interact with αPS2/βPS integrin (Chanana et al., 2007; Subramanian et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chanana et al., 2007; Subramanian et al., 2007.

claim: Both mouse Thbs4 and Drosophila Tsp rescued the reduced life span in the Sgcd840 MD Drosophila line.
source: Remarkably, both Thbs4 and Tsp rescued the reduced life span in the Sgcd840 MD Drosophila line, and normalized muscle function as assessed with a negative geotaxis assay (Figure 8A,B; Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 8A and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Both mouse Thbs4 and Drosophila Tsp normalized muscle function in the Sgcd840 MD Drosophila line as assessed with a negative geotaxis assay.
source: Remarkably, both Thbs4 and Tsp rescued the reduced life span in the Sgcd840 MD Drosophila line, and normalized muscle function as assessed with a negative geotaxis assay (Figure 8A,B; Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by negative geotaxis data shown in Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The rupture of the dorsal median indirect flight muscles and their loss of proper ectoskeletal attachment were rescued by muscle-specific overexpression of either mouse Thbs4 or Drosophila Tsp.
source: The rupture of the dorsal median indirect flight muscles and their loss of proper ectoskeletal attachment were also rescued by muscle-specific overexpression of either mouse Thbs4 or Drosophila Tsp (Figure 8C; Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 8C and Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Thbs4 or Tsp overexpression was exclusively restricted to a vesicular compartment within the indirect flight muscles of these overexpressing Tg lines, but not outside the myofibers.
source: Mechanistically, Thbs4 or Tsp overexpression was exclusively restricted to a vesicular compartment within the indirect flight muscles of these overexpressing Tg lines, but not outside the myofibers (Figure 8D,H; Figure 8—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and immunogold electron microscopy data shown in Figure 8D, 8H, and Figure 8—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Both mouse Thbs4 and Drosophila Tsp overexpression produced noticeably greater levels of membrane βPS integrin localization in Drosophila muscle.
source: More provocatively, both mouse Thbs4 and Drosophila Tsp overexpression produced noticeably greater levels of membrane βPS integrin localization in Drosophila muscle (Figure 8E,F; Figure 8—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and Western blot data shown in Figure 8E, 8F, and Figure 8—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: Ultrastructural analysis revealed a remarkable rescue of the sarcomeric tears in Sgcd840 Drosophila with the mouse Thbs4 or Drosophila Tsp Tg.
source: Ultrastructural analysis revealed a remarkable rescue of the sarcomeric tears in Sgcd840Drosophila with the mouse Thbs4 or Drosophila Tsp Tg, although without inducing ER-stress nor ER and post-ER vesicular expansion in these muscles (Figure 8F,G; Figure 8—figure supplement 1G–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 8G and Figure 8—figure supplement 1G–I.

claim: Mouse Thbs4 or Drosophila Tsp overexpression in Sgcd840 Drosophila did not induce ER-stress nor ER and post-ER vesicular expansion in these muscles.
source: Ultrastructural analysis revealed a remarkable rescue of the sarcomeric tears in Sgcd840Drosophila with the mouse Thbs4 or Drosophila Tsp Tg, although without inducing ER-stress nor ER and post-ER vesicular expansion in these muscles (Figure 8F,G; Figure 8—figure supplement 1G–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot and transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 8F, 8G, and Figure 8—figure supplement 1G–I.

claim: Thbs proteins underlie an ancient program for membrane stabilization through regulation of intracellular attachment protein complexes and their content at the surface membrane.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that Thbs proteins underlie an ancient program for membrane stabilization through regulation of intracellular attachment protein complexes and their content at the surface membrane, although ER expansion through ATF6α appears to have evolved phylogenetically after Drosophila.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the conservation of Thbs function in both mice and Drosophila.

claim: ER expansion through ATF6α appears to have evolved phylogenetically after Drosophila.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that Thbs proteins underlie an ancient program for membrane stabilization through regulation of intracellular attachment protein complexes and their content at the surface membrane, although ER expansion through ATF6α appears to have evolved phylogenetically after Drosophila.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that Thbs/Tsp overexpression in Drosophila does not induce ER expansion.
